topics.name: Introduction
topics.description: Open Claw is a self-hosted AI agent gateway that connects your messaging apps to AI models you control. You run a single Gateway process on your own machine or server, and it becomes the bridge between platforms like Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Slack, Signal, and more, and an always-available AI assistant. It is MIT-licensed, open source, and designed for developers and power users who want a personal AI they can message from anywhere without giving up control of their data.

resources.title: What Is OpenClaw? The Open-Source AI Agent That Actually Does Things

subtopics.name: Gateway
subtopics.description: The Gateway is the single always-on process that handles routing, the control plane, and all channel connections. It runs on a single multiplexed port that serves the WebSocket control and RPC interface, HTTP APIs, the Control UI, and hooks. By default, it binds to localhost and requires an auth token before accepting any connections.

resources.title: OpenClaw Gateway: Setup, Start/Stop Commands & Remote Mode

subtopics.name: Agents
subtopics.description: An agent in Open Claw is a fully isolated unit with its own workspace folder containing its personality and configuration files, its own state directory that holds auth profiles and the model registry, and its own session store that keeps the full conversation history separate from every other agent. Because auth profiles are scoped per-agent, credentials for one agent are never automatically shared with another, which means you can run a personal agent on your WhatsApp number and a work agent on a separate account on the same Gateway without any risk of their sessions, memories, or API keys crossing over.

subtopics.name: Agent Loop
subtopics.description: When Open Claw receives a message, it runs a full agent loop rather than returning a single response. The loop validates the message, resolves the model, assembles the system prompt from skills and context files, and then sends everything to the model for inference. If the model decides to call a tool, like running a command, reading a file, or searching the web, the loop executes it, feeds the result back to the model, and continues until no more tool calls are needed and a final reply is ready. If the session gets too long for the context window, compaction kicks in automatically before retrying.

subtopics.name: Context Window
subtopics.description: The context window is the amount of conversation history, instructions, and tool results the AI model can see at once when generating a response. Open Claw manages this carefully through a context engine and compaction system so long-running agents don't exceed the model's limits.

resources.title: OpenClaw Memory Masterclass: The complete guide to agent memory that survives • VelvetShark

subtopics.name: Channels
subtopics.description: Channels are the messaging platforms through which users interact with Open Claw, and each one connects to the single Gateway process that routes incoming messages to the right agent and sends replies back. Every channel runs simultaneously on the same Gateway, so you can be connected to Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, and Slack all at once without running separate processes. Text is supported across all channels, but richer features like reactions, media, message editing, and group behavior vary depending on what each platform's API supports

subtopics.name: Skills
subtopics.description: OpenClaw uses AgentSkills-compatible skill folders to teach the agent how to use tools. A skill is a markdown file injected into the system prompt that gives the agent context, constraints, and step-by-step guidance for using tools effectively. Skills live in your workspace, in shared folders, or ship inside plugins.

resources.title: What are OpenClaw Skills? A 2026 Developer’s Guide | DigitalOcean

subtopics.name: Memory System
subtopics.description: The memory system allows Open Claw agents to remember information across conversations. Instead of starting fresh every time, agents can store and retrieve facts, past interactions, or user preferences from structured memory files in the workspace. Open Claw also includes a compaction system that automatically summarizes older conversation history when a session grows too long, preserving the essential information while freeing up space for new exchanges.

subtopics.name: Proactive Core
subtopics.description: The proactive core is what allows Open Claw agents to act on their own initiative rather than just responding to messages. Using heartbeats, cron jobs, and standing orders, the agent can run tasks on a schedule or trigger automatically based on conditions you define.

resources.title: How OpenClaw Works: Understanding AI Agents Through a Real Architecture

OpenClaw is a community-built alternative that runs independently, supports a wide range of AI providers beyond Anthropic, and extends beyond coding to general agent automation across messaging platforms.

subtopics.name: Use cases
subtopics.description: Open Claw can be used for a wide range of tasks: you can connect it to your messaging apps to have it read and respond to messages on your behalf, set up scheduled jobs using cron and heartbeats to run recurring tasks like daily summaries or file cleanups without any human input, process incoming data from webhooks by extracting and acting on information automatically, manage and update files and documentation in your workspace, chain multiple actions together in a single agent loop to complete multi-step workflows from start to finish, and even run several specialized agents in parallel with routing rules and shared memory so each one handles a different domain while staying coordinated with the others.

topics.description: Open Claw runs a single long-lived Gateway that owns all messaging surfaces and exposes a typed WebSocket API for control-plane clients like the macOS app, CLI, and web UI. When a message arrives, the Gateway routes it to the appropriate agent, which then runs through a full loop of context assembly, model inference, and tool execution before streaming a reply back.

subtopics.name: Why and Why not?
subtopics.description: A local machine is the right choice if you are just getting started, experimenting with Open Claw, or running it as a personal assistant for yourself only. It requires no ongoing costs, no remote infrastructure to manage, and lets you get up and running in minutes. It is not a good fit if you need your agent to be available 24/7, reachable from outside your home network, or capable of receiving webhooks from external services, since your agent goes offline whenever your machine is off or asleep and most home networks block incoming traffic by default.

subtopics.name: Security Best Practices
subtopics.description: Use a local machine setup only for single-user personal use. Bind the Gateway to localhost so it is never exposed to the internet, set a strong randomly generated auth token, and store all API keys in environment variables rather than config files. Run Open Claw as a non-root user, keep your sender allowlist to just yourself, and enable device pairing so unknown devices cannot connect. Run `openclaw security audit --deep` after any configuration change and keep Open Claw updated regularly.

It is the most common production setup and works well for personal assistants, team automation, and any workflow that requires continuous availability. It is not a good fit if you want to avoid recurring costs, prefer to keep everything on hardware you physically own, or want to run local models via Ollama without paying for a powerful enough remote machine.

subtopics.name: Security Best Practices
subtopics.description: When running Open Claw locally, bind the Gateway to localhost only so it is never exposed directly to the internet, set a strong, randomly generated auth token, and never hardcode API keys in config files — use environment variables instead. Run the process as a non-root user, keep your sender allowlist minimal, and enable device pairing so unknown devices cannot connect. Be cautious about prompt injection since the agent can read external content like emails and web pages. Run `openclaw security audit --deep` after any configuration change, keep Open Claw updated regularly, and rotate all credentials immediately if you suspect a breach.

topics.name: Installation
topics.description: Installation covers the steps to get Open Claw onto your chosen environment. It requires a recent version of Node.js, an API key from your chosen model provider, and takes around five minutes. The core install command is `npm install -g openclaw@latest`, after which you run openclaw onboard to connect your first model and channel. Always check the official documentation for the current Node.js version requirements before installing, as these may change between releases.

It shines most in dedicated hardware setups like a Mac Mini or a capable home server, where you have enough RAM and processing power to run a model comfortably. However, low-powered devices like a Raspberry Pi will likely struggle with most models.

subtopics.description: Workspace settings define the environment your agent operates in, including its identity, behavioral guidelines, and what it knows about you. These are stored in a set of markdown configuration files in your project directory.

subtopics.name: SOUL.md
subtopics.description: [SOUL.md](http://SOUL.md) is the file where you define the agent's personality, tone, and core behavioral guidelines. Think of it as the agent's character sheet. It shapes how it communicates and makes decisions across all conversations.

subtopics.name: MEMORY.md
subtopics.description: [MEMORY.md](http://MEMORY.md) is a persistent file where the agent stores important facts it has learned over time. It is regularly updated so the agent can recall relevant information in future conversations.

subtopics.name: memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md
subtopics.description: These are dated memory log files that store a record of what happened on a specific day. They give the agent a chronological history that it can reference when needed, and are created automatically by the session-memory hook.

subtopics.name: Other Workspace Files
subtopics.description: Open Claw recognizes several other special markdown files that are automatically injected into the agent's context at startup. [BOOT.md](http://BOOT.md) contains instructions that the agent runs once when the Gateway starts. [TOOLS.md](http://TOOLS.md) describes the tools available to the agent and how they should be used. [IDENTITY.md](http://IDENTITY.md) is an alternative or complement to [SOUL.md](http://SOUL.md) for defining the agent's persona. [BOOTSTRAP.md](http://BOOTSTRAP.md) is a general-purpose file for injecting additional context into every session. On top of these recognized filenames, you can also add any other markdown files to your workspace, such as project notes, reference documents, or custom instructions for specific tasks.

resources.title: AI Agents 003 — OpenClaw Workspace Files Explained: SOUL.md, AGENTS.md, HEARTBEAT.md and More

subtopics.name: AGENTS.md
subtopics.description: [AGENTS.md](http://AGENTS.md) describes the agents available in your workspace, their roles, and how they relate to each other. It is used when running multiple agents to clarify who does what.

subtopics.name: Gateway Settings
subtopics.description: Gateway settings control how the Open Claw server behaves, including the port it listens on, authentication tokens, and which interfaces it binds to. These settings are critical for both functionality and security.

subtopics.name: USER.md
subtopics.description: [USER.md](http://USER.md) contains information about you: your preferences, context, and anything you want the agent to know about you by default. The agent reads this to personalize its responses.

topics.name: Hooks
topics.description: Hooks are small scripts that run inside the Gateway when specific agent events fire, like `/new`, `/reset`, `/stop`, or lifecycle events. They are automatically discovered from directories and can be inspected with `openclaw hooks`.

subtopics.description: WhatsApp is the most popular channel in Open Claw. It connects via the Baileys library and requires a QR code pairing step to link your account to the Gateway.

subtopics.name: Hook Structure
subtopics.description: Each hook is a directory containing a `HOOK.md` file with metadata and a `handler.ts` file with the logic to run. The metadata defines which events to listen for and what requirements the hook needs to be eligible.

topics.name: Webhooks
topics.description: Webhooks allow external services to send HTTP requests to Open Claw to trigger agent actions. This is how you can connect third-party tools like GitHub or custom apps to your agent.

subtopics.name: Event Types
subtopics.description: Open Claw hooks support a range of event types, including command events like `/new` and `/reset`, session events like compaction, agent bootstrap events, gateway startup events, and message received and sent events.

topics.name: Usage Best Practices
topics.description: To get the most out of Open Claw, run `openclaw doctor` regularly to catch configuration drift early, and always run openclaw `security audit --deep` after any config change. Keep your workspace files like [SOUL.md](http://SOUL.md), [USER.md](http://USER.md), and [MEMORY.md](http://MEMORY.md) up to date so the agent always has accurate context about who you are and how you want it to behave. Use `/new` at the start of a new topic rather than letting a single session grow indefinitely, which keeps the context window clean and triggers the session-memory hook to save what was discussed. Start with a minimal tool allowlist and only expand permissions when you have a specific need, and prefer Tailscale over open ports for any remote access to keep your Gateway secure without extra complexity.

subtopics.name: Adding Daemon
subtopics.description: A daemon is a background process that runs continuously without needing a terminal window open. Configuring Open Claw as a daemon ensures it starts automatically and keeps running even after you log out or restart your machine.

You can add the `--yes` flag to automatically accept any prompts without manual input, which is useful for running the command in a headless or

subtopics.name: gateway
subtopics.description: `openclaw gateway` is the main command for interacting with the gateway process. It is the entry point for all gateway-related operations from the command line.

subtopics.name: gateway start | stop | restart
subtopics.description: `openclaw gateway start`, `openclaw gateway stop`, and `openclaw gateway restart` control the lifecycle of the Open Claw gateway process, starting it up, shutting it down, or restarting it after a configuration change.

subtopics.name: channels list
subtopics.description: `openclaw channels list` displays all the communication channels currently connected to your Open Claw gateway, along with their status.

subtopics.name: channels login
subtopics.description: `openclaw channels login` initiates the authentication flow for a specific channel, allowing Open Claw to connect to it on your behalf.

subtopics.name: channels add --channel
subtopics.description: `openclaw channels add --channel` adds a new communication channel to your Open Claw setup, specifying which platform to connect.

subtopics.name: channels remove --channel
subtopics.description: `openclaw channels remove --channel` disconnects and removes a channel from your Open Claw configuration.

subtopics.name: channels status --probe
subtopics.description: `openclaw channels status --probe` actively checks the connection status of your channels by probing them, rather than just reporting cached status.

subtopics.name: models list | set | status
subtopics.description: `openclaw models list`, `openclaw models set`, and `openclaw models status` let you view the AI models available in your setup, switch between them, and check which one is currently active.

subtopics.name: models auth add
subtopics.description: `openclaw models auth add` is the interactive auth helper. It can launch a provider auth flow (OAuth/API key) or guide you into manual token paste, depending on the provider you choose.

subtopics.name: models auth setup-token
subtopics.description: `openclaw models auth setup-token` stores the authentication token for a model provider, allowing Open Claw to make authenticated API calls on your behalf. It is part of the broader `models auth` command group, which also includes `add`, `login`, and `paste-token`.

subtopics.name: cron list
subtopics.description: `openclaw cron list` shows all the scheduled tasks currently registered in Open Claw along with their schedules and status.

subtopics.name: cron add
subtopics.description: `openclaw cron add` registers a new scheduled task, letting you define what the agent should do and when it should trigger automatically.

subtopics.name: memory index --all
subtopics.description: `openclaw memory index` rebuilds the search index for all memory files, ensuring the agent can efficiently retrieve relevant information from its stored memories.

subtopics.name: memory search "<query>"
subtopics.description: `openclaw memory search "query"` lets you search through the agent's stored memories using a keyword or phrase, useful for checking what the agent has remembered about past conversations or preferences.

subtopics.name: backup create
subtopics.description: `openclaw backup create` generates a snapshot of your Open Claw configuration and memory files so you can restore your setup if something goes wrong.

topics.name: Heartbeats
topics.description: Heartbeats are periodic signals the Gateway emits on a regular interval. They can be used to confirm the agent is alive and to trigger recurring background tasks without any human input.

resources.title: OpenClaw Cron Jobs vs Heartbeat Explained

subtopics.name: Securing Webhooks
subtopics.description: The Webhooks plugin ensures that each route is protected by shared-secret authentication, rate limiting, request size guards, and in-flight request limiting. Use a strong unique secret per route, store it as a SecretRef rather than inline plaintext, and bind each route to the narrowest session that fits the workflow. If a secret cannot be resolved at startup, the plugin skips that route and logs a warning instead of exposing a broken endpoint.

subtopics.name: Interval & Active Hours
subtopics.description: You can configure how often heartbeats fire and restrict them to certain hours of the day, so your agent only runs automated tasks during times you define as active.

topics.name: Automating Tasks
topics.description: Open Claw supports several mechanisms for running tasks automatically, including hooks, webhooks, heartbeats, and cron jobs, so your agent can act without waiting for a human to send a message.

topics.name: Cron Jobs
topics.description: Cron jobs are scheduled tasks that run at specific times or intervals. They allow you to automate recurring actions like summaries, cleanups, or reports without any human prompt.

subtopics.description: [HEARTBEAT.md](http://HEARTBEAT.md) is a workspace configuration file where you define what the agent should do during each heartbeat cycle — essentially a set of instructions for proactive, time-based behavior.

subtopics.name: Managing & Disabling Jobs
subtopics.description: You can list, pause, and delete cron jobs from the command line, giving you control over which scheduled tasks are active at any given time.

subtopics.name: Creating Skills
subtopics.description: You can write your own skills by creating a `SKILL.md` file with instructions and placing it in your workspace's `skills/` folder. This lets you teach the agent new behaviors tailored to your specific needs.

topics.name: Sessions
topics.description: A session is the conversation context tied to a specific agent and chat source. Direct messages share one session by default, but you can isolate each sender into their own context, strongly recommended if more than one person can message your agent. All session state is owned by the Gateway and maintained automatically through pruning and entry caps to keep the store bounded over time.

topics.name: Skills
topics.description: Skills are modular capability packages that extend what your agent can do. Each skill is a markdown file injected into the system prompt that gives the agent context and guidance for using specific tools or following specific workflows.

resources.title: What are OpenClaw Skills? A 2026 Developer’s Guide

topics.name: Plugins
topics.description: Plugins are packages that can register any combination of capabilities: channels, model providers, tools, skills, speech, image generation, and more. Some are bundled with Open Claw, and others are published by the community on npm.

resources.title: Create OpenClaw AI Plugin for Extra Features and Skills | Step-by-Step Guide for Beginners

subtopics.name: Installing Plugins
subtopics.description: Plugins are installed via `openclaw plugins install` followed by the package name or path. Once installed, they become available to all agents in your workspace.

subtopics.name: Creating Plugins
subtopics.description: You can build your own plugins to add custom functionality to Open Claw, such as integrating a new service or adding a new type of tool the agent can call.

subtopics.name: Security Risks
subtopics.description: Plugins run at a deeper level than skills and can have significant access to your system. Open Claw installs plugin dependencies with `--ignore-scripts` to reduce risk, but you should still only install plugins from trusted sources.

resources.title: OpenClaw Security: 12 Best Practices Our Experts Recommend

topics.name: MCP
topics.description: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI models to external tools and data sources. Open Claw supports MCP, allowing your agent to call tools from any MCP-compatible server.

resources.title: How to Set Up OpenClaw MCP Server

topics.name: Multi-Agents
topics.description: Multi-agent mode lets you run several specialized agents in the same Open Claw gateway, each with its own workspace, auth profiles, and session store. They can operate independently or be coordinated through routing rules and shared memory.

subtopics.name: Routing Rules
subtopics.description: Routing rules determine which agent handles which incoming messages. Open Claw uses a deterministic, most-specific-wins system: peer matches beat channel-wide rules, which beat the fallback default agent.

subtopics.name: /new
subtopics.description: `/new` starts a fresh conversation with the agent, clearing the current context so you are beginning from a clean slate. It also triggers the session-memory hook to save the previous session before resetting. You can optionally pass a model name after `/new` to start the session with a specific model.

subtopics.name: /status
subtopics.description: `/status` asks the agent to report its current state, including active tasks, connected channels, and any pending operations. It also shows provider usage and quota for the current model provider when usage tracking is enabled.

subtopics.name: /model
subtopics.description: `/model` is a directive that lets you switch the AI model the agent is currently using. You can pass a number from the model picker, a full `provider/model` string, or use `/model list` to see available options.

subtopics.name: /context
subtopics.description: `/context` explains what context the agent is currently working with. You can use `/context list` for a summary, `/context detail` for a breakdown of per-file, per-tool, per-skill, and system prompt sizes, or `/context json` for machine-readable output.

subtopics.name: /compact
subtopics.description: `/compact` is a text-only command that compresses or summarizes the current conversation context to free up space in the context window without losing essential information. You can optionally pass instructions to guide how the compaction is done.

subtopics.name: /help
subtopics.description: `/help` displays a list of available slash commands and a brief description of what each one does. It also works as an inline shortcut, meaning it can be embedded in a normal message and will be stripped before the model sees the rest of the text.

subtopics.name: /stop
subtopics.description: `/stop` interrupts the agent if it is currently in the middle of a task or loop, bringing it to a halt immediately. It targets the active chat session directly so it can abort the current run.

subtopics.name: /reset
subtopics.description: `/reset` resets the agent's current state, clearing any ongoing task or context and returning it to its idle state. Like `/new`, it triggers the session-memory hook before resetting.

subtopics.name: /usage
subtopics.description: `/usage` controls the per-response usage footer appended to normal replies. It takes `off`, `tokens`, `full`, or `cost` as arguments. `/usage cost` prints a local cost summary from your Open Claw session logs rather than appending it to each reply.

subtopics.name: /think
subtopics.description: `/think` is a directive that sets the agent's thinking level before responding. It takes `off`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, or `xhigh` as arguments. Higher levels make the agent reason more deeply before giving a final answer, which is useful for complex or ambiguous tasks. Aliases: `/thinking`, `/t`.

subtopics.name: /fast
subtopics.description: `/fast` is a directive that toggles fast mode for the current session. It takes `on`, `off`, or `status` as arguments. Fast mode maps to different provider-level behaviors depending on your model — for example, `service_tier=priority` on OpenAI or `service_tier=auto` on Anthropic. Omitting the argument shows the current effective fast-mode state.

subtopics.name: /reasoning
subtopics.description: `/reasoning` is a directive that enables or disables extended reasoning mode. It takes `on`, `off`, or `stream` as arguments. When set to `on`, the agent sends a separate message prefixed with `Reasoning:` before its final reply. `stream` enables Telegram draft streaming only. Alias: `/reason`.

subtopics.name: /config
subtopics.description: `/config` reads and writes your on-disk `openclaw.json` configuration file directly from chat. It is disabled by default and requires `commands.config: true` in your config to enable. It supports `show`, `get`, `set`, and `unset` subcommands and is owner-only.

subtopics.name: /allowlist
subtopics.description: `/allowlist` lists, adds, or removes entries from the sender allowlist that controls who can interact with the agent. Add and remove operations require `commands.config: true` to be set in your configuration.

subtopics.name: /mcp
subtopics.description: `/mcp` manages OpenClaw-managed MCP server definitions from chat. It is disabled by default and requires `commands.mcp: true` to enable. It supports `show`, `get`, `set`, and `unset` subcommands and is owner-only

subtopics.name: /plugins
subtopics.description: `/plugins` lets you inspect discovered plugins and toggle their enablement from chat. It is disabled by default and requires `commands.plugins: true` to enable. It supports `list`, `show`, `install`, `enable`, and `disable` subcommands. Write operations are owner-only. Alias: `/plugin`.

nodes.name: Introduction
nodes.description: Open Claw is a self-hosted AI agent gateway that connects your messaging apps to AI models you control. You run a single Gateway process on your own machine or server, and it becomes the bridge between platforms like Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Slack, Signal, and more, and an always-available AI assistant. It is MIT-licensed, open source, and designed for developers and power users who want a personal AI they can message from anywhere without giving up control of their data.

resources.title: What Is OpenClaw? The Open-Source AI Agent That Actually Does Things

nodes.name: Gateway
nodes.description: The Gateway is the single always-on process that handles routing, the control plane, and all channel connections. It runs on a single multiplexed port that serves the WebSocket control and RPC interface, HTTP APIs, the Control UI, and hooks. By default, it binds to localhost and requires an auth token before accepting any connections.

resources.title: OpenClaw Gateway: Setup, Start/Stop Commands & Remote Mode

nodes.name: Agents
nodes.description: An agent in Open Claw is a fully isolated unit with its own workspace folder containing its personality and configuration files, its own state directory that holds auth profiles and the model registry, and its own session store that keeps the full conversation history separate from every other agent. Because auth profiles are scoped per-agent, credentials for one agent are never automatically shared with another, which means you can run a personal agent on your WhatsApp number and a work agent on a separate account on the same Gateway without any risk of their sessions, memories, or API keys crossing over.

nodes.name: Agent Loop
nodes.description: When Open Claw receives a message, it runs a full agent loop rather than returning a single response. The loop validates the message, resolves the model, assembles the system prompt from skills and context files, and then sends everything to the model for inference. If the model decides to call a tool, like running a command, reading a file, or searching the web, the loop executes it, feeds the result back to the model, and continues until no more tool calls are needed and a final reply is ready. If the session gets too long for the context window, compaction kicks in automatically before retrying.

nodes.name: Context Window
nodes.description: The context window is the amount of conversation history, instructions, and tool results the AI model can see at once when generating a response. Open Claw manages this carefully through a context engine and compaction system so long-running agents don't exceed the model's limits.

resources.title: OpenClaw Memory Masterclass: The complete guide to agent memory that survives • VelvetShark

nodes.name: Channels
nodes.description: Channels are the messaging platforms through which users interact with Open Claw, and each one connects to the single Gateway process that routes incoming messages to the right agent and sends replies back. Every channel runs simultaneously on the same Gateway, so you can be connected to Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, and Slack all at once without running separate processes. Text is supported across all channels, but richer features like reactions, media, message editing, and group behavior vary depending on what each platform's API supports

nodes.name: Skills
nodes.description: OpenClaw uses AgentSkills-compatible skill folders to teach the agent how to use tools. A skill is a markdown file injected into the system prompt that gives the agent context, constraints, and step-by-step guidance for using tools effectively. Skills live in your workspace, in shared folders, or ship inside plugins.

resources.title: What are OpenClaw Skills? A 2026 Developer’s Guide | DigitalOcean

nodes.name: Memory System
nodes.description: The memory system allows Open Claw agents to remember information across conversations. Instead of starting fresh every time, agents can store and retrieve facts, past interactions, or user preferences from structured memory files in the workspace. Open Claw also includes a compaction system that automatically summarizes older conversation history when a session grows too long, preserving the essential information while freeing up space for new exchanges.

nodes.name: Proactive Core
nodes.description: The proactive core is what allows Open Claw agents to act on their own initiative rather than just responding to messages. Using heartbeats, cron jobs, and standing orders, the agent can run tasks on a schedule or trigger automatically based on conditions you define.

resources.title: How OpenClaw Works: Understanding AI Agents Through a Real Architecture

OpenClaw is a community-built alternative that runs independently, supports a wide range of AI providers beyond Anthropic, and extends beyond coding to general agent automation across messaging platforms.

nodes.name: Use cases
nodes.description: Open Claw can be used for a wide range of tasks: you can connect it to your messaging apps to have it read and respond to messages on your behalf, set up scheduled jobs using cron and heartbeats to run recurring tasks like daily summaries or file cleanups without any human input, process incoming data from webhooks by extracting and acting on information automatically, manage and update files and documentation in your workspace, chain multiple actions together in a single agent loop to complete multi-step workflows from start to finish, and even run several specialized agents in parallel with routing rules and shared memory so each one handles a different domain while staying coordinated with the others.

nodes.name: How OpenClaw Works
nodes.description: Open Claw runs a single long-lived Gateway that owns all messaging surfaces and exposes a typed WebSocket API for control-plane clients like the macOS app, CLI, and web UI. When a message arrives, the Gateway routes it to the appropriate agent, which then runs through a full loop of context assembly, model inference, and tool execution before streaming a reply back.

It requires no ongoing costs, no remote infrastructure to manage, and lets you get up and running in minutes. It is not a good fit if you need your agent to be available 24/7, reachable from outside your home network, or capable of receiving webhooks from external services, since your agent goes offline whenever your machine is off or asleep and most home networks block incoming traffic by default.

nodes.name: Security Best Practices
nodes.description: Use a local machine setup only for single-user personal use. Bind the Gateway to localhost so it is never exposed to the internet, set a strong randomly generated auth token, and store all API keys in environment variables rather than config files. Run Open Claw as a non-root user, keep your sender allowlist to just yourself, and enable device pairing so unknown devices cannot connect. Run `openclaw security audit --deep` after any configuration change and keep Open Claw updated regularly.

It is the most common production setup and works well for personal assistants, team automation, and any workflow that requires continuous availability. Run the process as a non-root user, keep your sender allowlist minimal, and enable device pairing so unknown devices cannot connect. Be cautious about prompt injection since the agent can read external content like emails and web pages. Run `openclaw security audit --deep` after any configuration change, keep Open Claw updated regularly, and rotate all credentials immediately if you suspect a breach.

nodes.name: SOUL.md
nodes.description: [SOUL.md](http://SOUL.md) is the file where you define the agent's personality, tone, and core behavioral guidelines. Think of it as the agent's character sheet. It shapes how it communicates and makes decisions across all conversations.

nodes.name: MEMORY.md
nodes.description: [MEMORY.md](http://MEMORY.md) is a persistent file where the agent stores important facts it has learned over time. It is regularly updated so the agent can recall relevant information in future conversations.

nodes.name: memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md
nodes.description: These are dated memory log files that store a record of what happened on a specific day. They give the agent a chronological history that it can reference when needed, and are created automatically by the session-memory hook.

nodes.name: Other Workspace Files
nodes.description: Open Claw recognizes several other special markdown files that are automatically injected into the agent's context at startup. [BOOT.md](http://BOOT.md) contains instructions that the agent runs once when the Gateway starts. [TOOLS.md](http://TOOLS.md) describes the tools available to the agent and how they should be used. [IDENTITY.md](http://IDENTITY.md) is an alternative or complement to [SOUL.md](http://SOUL.md) for defining the agent's persona. [BOOTSTRAP.md](http://BOOTSTRAP.md) is a general-purpose file for injecting additional context into every session. On top of these recognized filenames, you can also add any other markdown files to your workspace, such as project notes, reference documents, or custom instructions for specific tasks.

resources.title: AI Agents 003 — OpenClaw Workspace Files Explained: SOUL.md, AGENTS.md, HEARTBEAT.md and More

nodes.name: AGENTS.md
nodes.description: [AGENTS.md](http://AGENTS.md) describes the agents available in your workspace, their roles, and how they relate to each other. It is used when running multiple agents to clarify who does what.

nodes.name: Gateway Settings
nodes.description: Gateway settings control how the Open Claw server behaves, including the port it listens on, authentication tokens, and which interfaces it binds to. These settings are critical for both functionality and security.

nodes.name: USER.md
nodes.description: [USER.md](http://USER.md) contains information about you: your preferences, context, and anything you want the agent to know about you by default. The agent reads this to personalize its responses.

nodes.name: Hooks
nodes.description: Hooks are small scripts that run inside the Gateway when specific agent events fire, like `/new`, `/reset`, `/stop`, or lifecycle events. They are automatically discovered from directories and can be inspected with `openclaw hooks`.

nodes.name: Hook Structure
nodes.description: Each hook is a directory containing a `HOOK.md` file with metadata and a `handler.ts` file with the logic to run. The metadata defines which events to listen for and what requirements the hook needs to be eligible.

nodes.name: Webhooks
nodes.description: Webhooks allow external services to send HTTP requests to Open Claw to trigger agent actions. This is how you can connect third-party tools like GitHub or custom apps to your agent.

nodes.name: Event Types
nodes.description: Open Claw hooks support a range of event types, including command events like `/new` and `/reset`, session events like compaction, agent bootstrap events, gateway startup events, and message received and sent events.

nodes.name: Usage Best Practices
nodes.description: To get the most out of Open Claw, run `openclaw doctor` regularly to catch configuration drift early, and always run openclaw `security audit --deep` after any config change. Keep your workspace files like [SOUL.md](http://SOUL.md), [USER.md](http://USER.md), and [MEMORY.md](http://MEMORY.md) up to date so the agent always has accurate context about who you are and how you want it to behave. Use `/new` at the start of a new topic rather than letting a single session grow indefinitely, which keeps the context window clean and triggers the session-memory hook to save what was discussed. Start with a minimal tool allowlist and only expand permissions when you have a specific need, and prefer Tailscale over open ports for any remote access to keep your Gateway secure without extra complexity.

nodes.name: doctor

nodes.name: gateway
nodes.description: `openclaw gateway` is the main command for interacting with the gateway process. It is the entry point for all gateway-related operations from the command line.

nodes.name: gateway start | stop | restart
nodes.description: `openclaw gateway start`, `openclaw gateway stop`, and `openclaw gateway restart` control the lifecycle of the Open Claw gateway process, starting it up, shutting it down, or restarting it after a configuration change.

nodes.name: channels list
nodes.description: `openclaw channels list` displays all the communication channels currently connected to your Open Claw gateway, along with their status.

nodes.name: channels login
nodes.description: `openclaw channels login` initiates the authentication flow for a specific channel, allowing Open Claw to connect to it on your behalf.

nodes.name: channels add --channel
nodes.description: `openclaw channels add --channel` adds a new communication channel to your Open Claw setup, specifying which platform to connect.

nodes.name: channels remove --channel
nodes.description: `openclaw channels remove --channel` disconnects and removes a channel from your Open Claw configuration.

nodes.name: channels status --probe
nodes.description: `openclaw channels status --probe` actively checks the connection status of your channels by probing them, rather than just reporting cached status.

nodes.name: models list | set | status
nodes.description: `openclaw models list`, `openclaw models set`, and `openclaw models status` let you view the AI models available in your setup, switch between them, and check which one is currently active.

nodes.name: models auth add

nodes.name: models auth setup-token
nodes.description: `openclaw models auth setup-token` stores the authentication token for a model provider, allowing Open Claw to make authenticated API calls on your behalf. It is part of the broader `models auth` command group, which also includes `add`, `login`, and `paste-token`.

nodes.name: cron list

nodes.name: cron add

nodes.name: memory index --all

nodes.name: memory search "<query>"

nodes.name: backup create

nodes.name: Heartbeats
nodes.description: Heartbeats are periodic signals the Gateway emits on a regular interval. They can be used to confirm the agent is alive and to trigger recurring background tasks without any human input.

nodes.name: Securing Webhooks
nodes.description: The Webhooks plugin ensures that each route is protected by shared-secret authentication, rate limiting, request size guards, and in-flight request limiting. Use a strong unique secret per route, store it as a SecretRef rather than inline plaintext, and bind each route to the narrowest session that fits the workflow. If a secret cannot be resolved at startup, the plugin skips that route and logs a warning instead of exposing a broken endpoint.

nodes.name: Interval & Active Hours
nodes.description: You can configure how often heartbeats fire and restrict them to certain hours of the day, so your agent only runs automated tasks during times you define as active.

nodes.name: Automating Tasks
nodes.description: Open Claw supports several mechanisms for running tasks automatically, including hooks, webhooks, heartbeats, and cron jobs, so your agent can act without waiting for a human to send a message.

nodes.name: Cron Jobs

nodes.name: HEARTBEAT.md
nodes.description: [HEARTBEAT.md](http://HEARTBEAT.md) is a workspace configuration file where you define what the agent should do during each heartbeat cycle — essentially a set of instructions for proactive, time-based behavior.

nodes.name: Managing & Disabling Jobs
nodes.description: You can list, pause, and delete cron jobs from the command line, giving you control over which scheduled tasks are active at any given time.

nodes.name: Creating Skills
nodes.description: You can write your own skills by creating a `SKILL.md` file with instructions and placing it in your workspace's `skills/` folder. This lets you teach the agent new behaviors tailored to your specific needs.

resources.title: Create Unlimited OpenClaw Skills | Full Tutorial (Upstage Studio Skill)

nodes.name: Installing from ClawHub
nodes.description: ClawHub is a community repository of pre-built skills. You can browse and install skills from ClawHub directly, saving time compared to building them from scratch.

nodes.name: Security Risks
nodes.description: Installing third-party skills carries risk since a skill can define instructions or tool access that could be misused. It is important to review skills from external sources before installing them.

resources.title: OpenClaw Security: 12 Best Practices Our Experts Recommend

nodes.name: Sessions
nodes.description: A session is the conversation context tied to a specific agent and chat source. Direct messages share one session by default, but you can isolate each sender into their own context, strongly recommended if more than one person can message your agent. All session state is owned by the Gateway and maintained automatically through pruning and entry caps to keep the store bounded over time.

nodes.name: Skills
nodes.description: Skills are modular capability packages that extend what your agent can do. Each skill is a markdown file injected into the system prompt that gives the agent context and guidance for using specific tools or following specific workflows.

resources.title: What are OpenClaw Skills? A 2026 Developer’s Guide
Everything You Need to Know About OpenClaw Skills (Beginner to Pro)

nodes.name: Plugins
nodes.description: Plugins are packages that can register any combination of capabilities: channels, model providers, tools, skills, speech, image generation, and more. Some are bundled with Open Claw, and others are published by the community on npm.

resources.title: Create OpenClaw AI Plugin for Extra Features and Skills | Step-by-Step Guide for Beginners

nodes.name: Installing Plugins
nodes.description: Plugins are installed via `openclaw plugins install` followed by the package name or path. Once installed, they become available to all agents in your workspace.

nodes.name: Creating Plugins
nodes.description: You can build your own plugins to add custom functionality to Open Claw, such as integrating a new service or adding a new type of tool the agent can call.

nodes.name: Security Risks
nodes.description: Plugins run at a deeper level than skills and can have significant access to your system. Open Claw installs plugin dependencies with `--ignore-scripts` to reduce risk, but you should still only install plugins from trusted sources.

resources.title: OpenClaw Security: 12 Best Practices Our Experts Recommend

nodes.name: MCP
nodes.description: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI models to external tools and data sources. Open Claw supports MCP, allowing your agent to call tools from any MCP-compatible server.

resources.title: How to Set Up OpenClaw MCP Server

nodes.name: Multi-Agents
nodes.description: Multi-agent mode lets you run several specialized agents in the same Open Claw gateway, each with its own workspace, auth profiles, and session store. They can operate independently or be coordinated through routing rules and shared memory.

nodes.name: Routing Rules
nodes.description: Routing rules determine which agent handles which incoming messages. Open Claw uses a deterministic, most-specific-wins system: peer matches beat channel-wide rules, which beat the fallback default agent.

nodes.name: /new
nodes.description: `/new` starts a fresh conversation with the agent, clearing the current context so you are beginning from a clean slate. It also triggers the session-memory hook to save the previous session before resetting. You can optionally pass a model name after `/new` to start the session with a specific model.

nodes.name: /status
nodes.description: `/status` asks the agent to report its current state, including active tasks, connected channels, and any pending operations. It also shows provider usage and quota for the current model provider when usage tracking is enabled.

nodes.name: /model
nodes.description: `/model` is a directive that lets you switch the AI model the agent is currently using. You can pass a number from the model picker, a full `provider/model` string, or use `/model list` to see available options.

nodes.name: /context
nodes.description: `/context` explains what context the agent is currently working with. You can use `/context list` for a summary, `/context detail` for a breakdown of per-file, per-tool, per-skill, and system prompt sizes, or `/context json` for machine-readable output.

nodes.name: /compact
nodes.description: `/compact` is a text-only command that compresses or summarizes the current conversation context to free up space in the context window without losing essential information. You can optionally pass instructions to guide how the compaction is done.

nodes.name: /help
nodes.description: `/help` displays a list of available slash commands and a brief description of what each one does. It also works as an inline shortcut, meaning it can be embedded in a normal message and will be stripped before the model sees the rest of the text.

nodes.name: /stop
nodes.description: `/stop` interrupts the agent if it is currently in the middle of a task or loop, bringing it to a halt immediately. It targets the active chat session directly so it can abort the current run.

nodes.name: /reset
nodes.description: `/reset` resets the agent's current state, clearing any ongoing task or context and returning it to its idle state. Like `/new`, it triggers the session-memory hook before resetting.

nodes.name: /usage
nodes.description: `/usage` controls the per-response usage footer appended to normal replies. It takes `off`, `tokens`, `full`, or `cost` as arguments. `/usage cost` prints a local cost summary from your Open Claw session logs rather than appending it to each reply.

nodes.name: /think
nodes.description: `/think` is a directive that sets the agent's thinking level before responding. It takes `off`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, or `xhigh` as arguments. Higher levels make the agent reason more deeply before giving a final answer, which is useful for complex or ambiguous tasks. Aliases: `/thinking`, `/t`.

nodes.name: /fast
nodes.description: `/fast` is a directive that toggles fast mode for the current session. It takes `on`, `off`, or `status` as arguments. Fast mode maps to different provider-level behaviors depending on your model — for example, `service_tier=priority` on OpenAI or `service_tier=auto` on Anthropic. Omitting the argument shows the current effective fast-mode state.

nodes.name: /reasoning
nodes.description: `/reasoning` is a directive that enables or disables extended reasoning mode. It takes `on`, `off`, or `stream` as arguments. When set to `on`, the agent sends a separate message prefixed with `Reasoning:` before its final reply. `stream` enables Telegram draft streaming only. Alias: `/reason`.

nodes.name: /config
nodes.description: `/config` reads and writes your on-disk `openclaw.json` configuration file directly from chat. It is disabled by default and requires `commands.config: true` in your config to enable. It supports `show`, `get`, `set`, and `unset` subcommands and is owner-only.

nodes.name: /allowlist
nodes.description: `/allowlist` lists, adds, or removes entries from the sender allowlist that controls who can interact with the agent. Add and remove operations require `commands.config: true` to be set in your configuration.

nodes.name: /mcp
nodes.description: `/mcp` manages OpenClaw-managed MCP server definitions from chat. It is disabled by default and requires `commands.mcp: true` to enable. It supports `show`, `get`, `set`, and `unset` subcommands and is owner-only

nodes.name: /plugins
nodes.description: `/plugins` lets you inspect discovered plugins and toggle their enablement from chat. It is disabled by default and requires `commands.plugins: true` to enable. It supports `list`, `show`, `install`, `enable`, and `disable` subcommands. Write operations are owner-only. Alias: `/plugin`.
